__inputs.description: The Grafana Cloud Prometheus/Mimir datasource — pick the one used for prometheus.remote_write.grafana_cloud in infra/alloy/config.alloy

title: Ocar — Overview
description: Single dashboard for the whole ASG fleet: at-a-glance health, RED-method golden signals for the API, fleet and autoscaling, DB pool and queues, Node.js runtime (file descriptors, event loop, memory), per-instance and per-container resources, and a live log stream. Edited here, applied with Terraform (infra/terraform/observability/dashboards.tf); fixed uid 'ocar-overview' so applies update it in place. Postgres metrics are not in Grafana (they are archived to S3, infra/alloy/config.alloy). Deployment markers come from the annotation the deploy workflow posts at every cutover (tags deploy, blue-green, cutover).

list.name: host
list.label: Server
list.description: Instance ids that reported host metrics in the selected time range (from Prometheus, so it always agrees with the panels; it was built from log labels before).

panels.title: Servers up
panels.description: Servers currently reporting up (count of up{instance="api:4000"} == 1). An instant query, so a terminated server's stale series cannot inflate the count.

panels.title: Requests / sec
panels.description: All HTTP requests handled by the API across the selected servers. The R in RED.

panels.title: p95 latency
panels.description: 95% of successful (2xx) requests are faster than this (all routes; latency buckets are kept for successful requests only). Green under 300 ms, amber to 500 ms, red above: 500 ms is the project target.

panels.title: 5xx rate
panels.description: Share of requests answered with a server error. Zero is the goal; red above 1%. Shows 0 when there are no errors.

panels.title: DB pool waiting
panels.description: Requests waiting for a database connection, summed over servers (pg_pool_connections{state="waiting"}). Should stay 0; anything above means the pool is saturated.

panels.title: Requests / server / min
panels.description: Average requests per minute each server handles. The autoscaler adds servers when the load balancer's requests per server stays above 1,000 per minute; amber from 700.

panels.title: Request rate by route
panels.description: sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])) by (route) — the R in RED.

panels.title: Error rate (5xx ratio)
panels.description: sum(rate(...{status_code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(...[5m])) — the E in RED. A route with zero traffic in the window shows no data, not a false 0%.

panels.title: Request duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Latency percentiles of successful (2xx) requests across the selected servers (buckets are kept for successful requests only; error responses are counted in the rate and error panels). Under 100 ms all land in the first bucket, so fast requests are measured coarsely.

panels.title: Servers over time (autoscaling activity)
panels.description: count(up{instance="api:4000"}): servers reporting up. Steps up when the autoscaler adds capacity and during a deployment (old and new colour overlap); deployment markers are drawn from the workflow annotations.

panels.title: Requests per server per minute (autoscale metric)
panels.description: Requests per minute handled by each server. The autoscaler adds servers when the load balancer's requests per server stays above 1,000 per minute (dashed red line); this is the same quantity measured at the API. One server comfortably handled 2,200/min at about 20% CPU in the 2026-10-17 tests, so the trigger is conservative for light read traffic.

panels.title: File descriptors (% of the limit)
panels.description: Open files and network connections as a share of what each API process may open (open / limit). Every rider and driver socket, database and Redis connection uses one. Near 100% the server refuses new connections while still looking up. Amber from 60%, red from 80% (the alert fires at 80% for 5 minutes).

panels.title: Event loop lag (p99)
panels.description: How late the API's single main thread is getting to its next turn. About 10 ms is healthy; above 100 ms every request on that server is slowing down together (CPU can still look fine). The alert fires above 250 ms for 5 minutes.

panels.title: Memory: heap used and process RSS
panels.description: Heap is the memory Node uses for objects; RSS is everything the process holds in RAM. A line that only climbs and never comes back down is a memory leak, and the container is eventually killed (dropping every connected socket).

panels.title: Time spent in garbage collection
panels.description: Share of each second Node spends pausing to free memory. Under 5% is normal; sustained higher values mean memory pressure and show up as latency spikes.

panels.title: pg.Pool connections by state
panels.description: pg_pool_connections{state=~"total|idle|waiting"} — a rising 'waiting' with flat 'total' at DATABASE_POOL_MAX means requests are queuing for a connection.

panels.title: BullMQ job counts by queue and state
panels.description: bullmq_queue_job_counts{state=~"waiting|active|delayed|failed"} — a queue stuck rising in 'waiting' or 'failed' needs attention.

panels.title: Database connections by pool (all servers)
panels.description: Connections the API holds open to the database, summed over the selected servers, per pool: requests (pg_pool_connections), background jobs (pg_worker_pool_connections) and reports (pg_analytics_pool_connections). The database allows 181 connections, 3 reserved, so about 178 are usable. With the pool caps in the runbook (8 + 6 + 2 per server) 8 servers, the most a deployment runs, can hold at most 128. Amber from 100 (the alert), red at 178.

panels.title: Waiting for a database connection, by pool
panels.description: Requests, background jobs or reports that had to wait because every connection in their pool was busy (largest value on any selected server). Should stay 0. A pool that waits more than about 5 seconds errors, so sustained waiting means the pool cap is too low for the load.

panels.title: CPU % by Instance
panels.description: 100 - idle%, broken out by the host label (EC2 instance ID) — a single aggregate number hides one hot instance behind a healthy average.

panels.title: Memory Working Set by Container
panels.description: container_memory_working_set_bytes -- non-reclaimable memory, what the kernel OOM-killer actually looks at, not container_memory_usage_bytes (which includes reclaimable page cache and overstates real pressure).

panels.title: Memory Usage as % of Limit by Container
panels.description: working_set / spec_memory_limit -- only meaningful for containers with mem_limit actually set in docker-compose.prod.yml (currently api, cadvisor); containers with no configured limit report 0 as their limit and will show no data here, not 0%.

panels.title: OOM Events by Container
panels.description: increase(container_oom_events_total) -- should be a flat zero line always. Any nonzero point means that container actually hit its mem_limit and was killed by the kernel; the direct answer to 'did a limit trip yet'.

panels.title: ocar-api logs
panels.description: {service="ocar", env="$env"} — same low-cardinality labels as MUST-DO #2. Filtered by the $env, $host, and $min_level dropdowns above (Pino numeric levels: 30=info, 40=warn, 50=error) — all are line/label filters, not extra Loki stream labels, so they cost nothing in stream cardinality. Click a trace_id field on any line, then paste it into a Tempo TraceQL query ({trace:id="..."}) to jump from a log to its trace.
